motion_heading: Any Consent to Search Was Not Voluntary

sentences.text: When the prosecution relies on consent to justify a warrantless search, it bears the burden of proving that the consent was freely and voluntarily given.
Whether consent was voluntary is determined from the totality of all the circumstances.
Consent is not voluntary if it was the product of duress or coercion, express or implied.
Questions phrased as “do you mind if” lead to ambiguous responses that “may inhibit the State’s ability to prove the unequivocal consent that the law requires.”
Consent given in submission to a claim of lawful authority to search is not voluntary.

“[A]cquiescence is not the same as freely given consent, and the State bears the burden of proving that the consent was untainted by any implicit threats or subtle coercion that may have existed under the circumstances.”
Repeated questioning “may become coercive” when police convey they will not accept “no.”

authority.name: 4 Wayne R. LaFave, Search and Seizure § 8.2(b), at 79 (6th ed. 2020)

sentences.text: Acquiescence is not the same as freely given consent.
Whether the person knew of the right to refuse is a factor in the voluntariness analysis.

In *Brown*, the Court of Appeals discussed the increasing frequency of drivers being questioned about drug possession and asked for consent to search, which the court characterized as “an apparently ongoing and unjustified infringement of the privacy rights of Alaska citizens.”

The court explained that “[s]tudies reveal that the vast majority of motorists who are subjected to this type of request will accede to the officer and allow the search,” making it less clear if such consent can be considered voluntary.

The court stated the trend was of such concern that Article I, Section 14 of the Alaska Constitution should perhaps “be interpreted to completely preclude requests for searches during a routine traffic stop unless the search is related to the ground for the stop or is otherwise supported by a reasonable suspicion of criminality.”
*Brown* did not decide whether to apply that rule to all traffic stops, but its reasoning is instructive in the totality analysis for whether consent was voluntary.

practice_notes: List every circumstance of the request, including how many officers, where they stood, whether weapons were visible, the exact words used, and whether your client had been told they were free to go.
If consent followed an unlawful stop or detention, argue it's also tainted as fruit of that illegality — a separate argument from voluntariness.
